The Best Sonoma Wines For Thanksgiving Dinner

By WineCountry Collective November 17, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 1:13
Instaread

Thanksgiving dinner has a little bit of everything: roasted turkey, buttery mashed potatoes, savory stuffing, tart cranberry sauce, and maybe a sweet potato casserole topped with marshmallows. Finding one wine that works with all of it? That’s a tall order. Luckily, you don’t need a different bottle for every dish. With a few well-chosen Sonoma wines, you can cover the entire meal, keep your guests happy, and spend more time enjoying Thanksgiving than worrying about what’s in everyone’s glass.

Here’s your guide to what to pour, what to pair it with, and how much wine you’ll actually need.

Start With the Thanksgiving MVP: Pinot Noir

If there’s one red wine that deserves a spot at your Thanksgiving table, it’s Pinot Noir. Especially Sonoma Coast Pinot Noir.

Unlike bigger reds that can overpower turkey, Pinot Noir has the acidity, fruit, and relatively gentle tannins to work with just about everything on the plate. Herb-roasted turkey? Absolutely. Mushroom stuffing? Even better. Cranberry sauce? Those bright red-fruit flavors can hold their own against its sweet-tart punch.

For a Sonoma pick, we’re looking to Coursey Graves Estate Winery, whose 2023 Sonoma Coast Pinot Noir is particularly suited to the Thanksgiving spread.

Located on Bennett Mountain, Coursey Graves produces small-lot wines that reflect Sonoma County’s diverse growing regions. The winery’s recently released holiday hosting guide highlights its Sonoma Coast Pinot Noir as a versatile dinner companion, especially with herb-roasted poultry, wild mushrooms, and seasonal vegetables. Here’s a peek at the Pinot Noir pairing card from the guide:

It’s a smart approach to Thanksgiving pairing. Rather than finding a wine for every side dish, choose one that can move comfortably between them.

Wines to Try:

  • Coursey Graves 2023 Sonoma Coast Pinot Noir, $85
  • Twomey 2024 Russian River Valley Pinot Noir, $60
  • DeLoach 2023 Green Valley Pinot Noir, $55

Hosting Tip: Hosting a big group? The WineCountry Private Cellar Holiday Table collection includes six food-friendly reds for $300 (regularly $650).

Let the Bubbles Flow Before Dinner

There’s a lot happening before Thanksgiving dinner hits the table. Guests are arriving, appetizers are circulating, and someone is inevitably asking when the turkey will be ready.

That’s your cue to open something sparkling.

A dry Sonoma sparkling wine is excellent with salty appetizers, creamy cheeses, and anything fried. Its refreshing acidity also works wonders against the richness of Thanksgiving food, so there’s no reason to stop pouring when dinner begins.

A standout choice is Iron Horse Vineyards’ 2021 Classic Vintage Brut, produced in the Green Valley of the Russian River Valley. Made from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, it offers notes of orchard fruit, toasted pastry, and a crisp finish. It’s especially good with cheese boards, baked brie, and buttery appetizers.

Wines to Try:

  • Iron Horse Vineyards 2021 Classic Vintage Brut, $58
  • Gloria Ferrer Sonoma Brut, $45
  • J Vineyards Cuvée 20 Brut, $40

Hosting Tip: Have the sparkling wine chilled before guests arrive. It’s one less thing to think about when the kitchen gets busy.

White Wines That Shine at Thanksgiving

Red wine may get much of the Thanksgiving attention, but a good white can be just as versatile. Chardonnay is a natural match for roasted turkey, buttery mashed potatoes, and creamy casseroles, while Sauvignon Blanc brings refreshing acidity that works beautifully with herb-heavy stuffing, green beans, and roasted vegetables.

For a Chardonnay that can handle just about anything on the Thanksgiving table, try Gary Farrell’s 2023 Ritchie Vineyard Chardonnay. With notes of golden apple, citrus, and subtle oak, it offers a balance of richness and freshness that works beautifully with roasted turkey, savory stuffing, and buttery sides.

Wines to Try:

  • Gary Farrell 2023 Ritchie Vineyard Chardonnay, $80
  • Coursey Graves 2023 Sonoma Coast Chardonnay, $70
  • Dry Creek Vineyard 2024 Fumé Blanc (Sauvignon Blanc), $21

Hosting Tip: Serve Sauvignon Blanc well chilled, but give Chardonnay a few minutes out of the refrigerator before pouring to let its flavors open up.

What About Guests Who Prefer a Bigger Red?

Not everyone wants Pinot Noir with their turkey. For guests who prefer something bolder, Sonoma County has plenty of delicious options, including Cabernet Sauvignon and Zinfandel.

The trick with Cabernet is choosing a balanced style rather than one with overpowering tannins. A well-made Sonoma Cab can be terrific alongside dark meat, rich gravy, sausage stuffing, and roasted mushrooms. Jordan’s elegant Alexander Valley Cabernet Sauvignon is a particularly good choice, offering ripe fruit and refined tannins without overwhelming the meal.

Zinfandel is another Thanksgiving favorite, especially when the menu includes glazed ham, savory stuffing, or sweet-and-spicy sides. Seghesio’s Sonoma Zinfandel brings juicy berry flavors and baking spice, making it a great option for those heartier holiday dishes.

Try Seghesio Family Vineyards’ 2024 Sonoma Zinfandel, which brings mixed-berry flavors, subtle baking spice, and soft tannins to the table.

Wines to Try:

  • Seghesio Family Vineyards 2024 Sonoma Zinfandel, $26
  • Jordan 2022 Alexander Valley Cabernet Sauvignon, $60

Hosting Tip: Not every bottle has to work with every dish. Sometimes the best pairing is simply the wine your guest enjoys most.

And cranberry sauce? It’s the wild card. Its sweetness and acidity can make dry wines taste sharper, so don’t worry about finding a perfect match. A fruit-forward Pinot Noir is a reasonable place to start.

How Much Wine Do You Need for Thanksgiving?

Now for the question that inevitably comes up while making the shopping list: how many bottles should you buy?

A standard 750ml bottle gives you approximately five 5-ounce glasses. If you’re planning on two glasses per wine-drinking adult, here’s a useful starting point:

How Much Wine to Buy

At Two Glasses per Wine-Drinking Guest

If you’re hosting a long afternoon or evening and expect three glasses per person, increase those amounts by about 50%.

For a group of eight, for example, you might choose one sparkling wine, one or two whites, and two reds, depending on your guests’ preferences. It’s often better to have a few extra bottles of popular styles than a dozen different wines with only one bottle each.

And make room for nonalcoholic drinks, too. Sparkling water, apple cider, and festive alcohol-free options deserve just as much attention.

A Few Serving Tips That Make a Big Difference

You’ve chosen the wines. Now don’t undo all that good work by serving the Pinot Noir at the temperature of your kitchen.

Here’s a simple temperature guide:

  • Sparkling wine: 40 to 50°F, well chilled.
  • Sauvignon Blanc: 45 to 50°F, chilled.
  • Chardonnay: 50 to 55°F, slightly less chilled to let its richer flavors come through.
  • Pinot Noir: 55 to 60°F, lightly cool.
  • Zinfandel and fuller reds: 60 to 65°F, cooler than most people’s idea of room temperature.

No wine refrigerator? No problem. Put your Pinot Noir in the fridge for about 20 minutes before serving.

As for decanting, unless you’re serving a particularly young, structured red or an older bottle with sediment, there’s little reason to add another step to your Thanksgiving preparations.

Save a Little Something for Dessert

By the time pumpkin pie arrives, you’ve probably already opened several bottles. Does dessert really need its own wine?

Not necessarily. But if you want to make dessert a separate occasion, a late-harvest Riesling or another sweet dessert wine can be delicious with apple pie or fruit-based desserts. Look for a wine that’s at least as sweet as the dessert itself.

Chocolate pecan pie is a different story. Its richness can work well with a sweet fortified wine, while pumpkin pie’s spices can complement a sweeter Riesling.

Or you could simply put on the coffee. After a big Thanksgiving dinner, that’s a perfectly respectable pairing, too.

The Best Thanksgiving Wine Plan? Keep It Simple.

A bottle of bubbles to start, a crisp white for the table, and a food-friendly Sonoma Pinot Noir will cover most Thanksgiving menus beautifully. Add something bolder if your guests love big reds, and you’ve got a lineup that works from appetizers to the last helping of stuffing.

The goal isn’t to impress everyone with an elaborate wine selection. It’s to pour something delicious, enjoy the food, and make a little more room for the people around the table.

After all, nobody remembers whether the Chardonnay was served at exactly 52 degrees. They remember the meal, and who they shared it with.
